stories.title: Quality Doesn’t Always Mean Newer Office Space
stories.excerpt: Steve Quick, Guckenheimer “Flight to quality” has been a recurring theme in the office market. As companies consolidate and upgrade workspaces, they’re looking for newer, flashier, heavily amenitized buildings to lure workers back to the office. Or so the headlines suggest. But for many occupiers, quality doesn’t mean newer. Experts told Connect CRE that many older office buildings can successfully compete for occupiers, especially when they offer the right combination of location, functionality and investment. “Flight to quality is still real. But I also don’t think there is one universal definition of quality, and I would be cautious about assuming that every occupier wants, or needs, the newest or flashiest asset,” said Steve Quick, Guckenheimer Americas’ CEO. In other words, the question occupiers ask might not be about age. Instead, the consideration is whether an office space works for business activities and employees. Age Isn’t Obsolescence Calling a building “older” can be misleading. A 40- or 50-year-old building can remain competitive if it has a strong location and has been well maintained and updated. Meanwhile, a newer building can struggle if it isn’t well-located or fails to meet occupier needs. The definition of “older” also depends on what has happened to a building since it was constructed. “I think older buildings might be considered those that haven’t been delivered or meaningfully renovated in the past five years, and don’t hold trophy Class A status,” said Michael Watts, CBRE’s President, Office Investor Leasing in the Americas. A building’s last upgrade might be more relevant to an occupier than its actual age. It can mean the difference between a functional workspace and inefficient systems. bullets: Office market shows 'flight to quality' is nuanced, not solely age-driven.
Well-maintained older buildings compete effectively with newer assets on location and functionality.
Occupier decision-making focuses on workspace utility and employee fit, not flashiness.
stories.summary: Industry experts push back on the assumption that all tenants demand newest, most amenitized office space. A 40–50 year-old building with strong location and proper maintenance can outcompete newer construction lacking those attributes. The defining factor is whether a space meets occupier business needs and employee requirements, not construction year or architectural novelty.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Signals softening demand for speculative office-to-residential conversions in secondary/tertiary markets where 'old building conversion value-play' thesis relies on flight-to-quality driving vacancies. However, strong office fundamentals in prime locations (SoHo, Lower Manhattan) may dampen conversion opportunity in top-tier markets.

stories.title: Newmark Arranges $85M Refi on Mixed-Use SoHo Property
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged an $85-million loan on behalf of InterVest Capital Partners to refinance 300 Lafayette St., a boutique mixed-use office and retail property in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood. Hudson Bay Capital provided the financing. Newmark Co-Head of Global Debt & Structured Finance Jordan Roeschlaub, Vice Chairman Nick Scribani, Managing Director John Caraviello and Associate Director Ryan Bub arranged the financing on behalf of the borrower. “300 Lafayette St. as good as boutique product gets in Lower Manhattan, new construction by COOKFOX with a fully occupied office component anchored by Microsoft and retail on one of the most heavily trafficked corners in SoHo,” said Scribani. “Lender interest was deep and competitive, and Zach Cion and the Hudson Bay Capital team delivered speed and certainty of execution for the sponsor.” Microsoft occupies the 63,000-square-foot entirety of the 82,000-square-foot property’s office component. Neko Health, New Era and Goldwin comprise the retail tenancy. The post Newmark Arranges $85M Refi on Mixed-Use SoHo Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Newmark arranges $85M refi on 300 Lafayette St., SoHo mixed-use with 63K SF Microsoft office.
Hudson Bay Capital provided financing; strong lender competition indicates debt market appetite for prime Manhattan boutique assets.
Property is new construction, 100% occupied office plus retail on high-traffic SoHo corner.
stories.summary: InterVest Capital Partners refinanced 300 Lafayette St. in Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood for $85 million through Hudson Bay Capital. The boutique mixed-use property features 63,000 square feet of office fully leased by Microsoft and ground-floor retail tenants including Neko Health, New Era, and Goldwin. Deep lender interest and competitive bidding underscore confidence in prime Lower Manhattan mixed-use assets.
stories.impact: Demonstrates sustained capital availability and risk appetite for trophy mixed-use in Manhattan's most desirable submarkets. Signals lenders view premium office + retail combos with anchor tenants (Microsoft) as core holdings, not distressed. This may constrain multifamily development capital competing for debt in NYC; prime mixed-use refinances absorb institutional lender capacity and set higher benchmarks for multifamily debt pricing in the same metro.

stories.title: Pistola Denim Takes Nearly 18K SF at ROW DTLA
stories.excerpt: Denim and womenswear company Pistola Denim has signed a 17,922-square-foot office lease at Atlas Capital Group’s ROW DTLA, adding another fashion company to the nearly 2 million-square-foot Downtown Los Angeles complex. Grace Na founded Pistola in 2013. The L.A.-based brand will move its creative team from warehouse and distribution space in Vernon. The terms of the lease were not disclosed. Karen Yi, ROW DTLA’s director of marketing and events, said Pistola joins other fashion brands at the property, which benefits from its proximity to L.A.’s Fashion District. Other office tenants include Adidas, Wilson, Revolve, Fashionphile, HOK, Day One Agency and MidFirst Bank. “Pistola has always been driven by creativity and collaboration, and we wanted a space that could really support that,” Na said in a statement. ROW DTLA spans 32 acres on the edge of the Arts District and includes more than 35 retailers, restaurants, wellness operators and event spaces. It was originally built in the 1920s around the former Los Angeles Terminal Market. But the seven former industrial buildings at the complex were redeveloped and reopened in 2017. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pistola Denim leases 17,922 SF office at ROW DTLA; moving creative team from Vernon warehouse.
Joins fashion-tenant cluster at 2M SF Downtown LA complex near Fashion District (Adidas, Revolve, Fashionphile).
Reflects corporate flight from industrial/warehouse space into branded mixed-use office in Arts District.
stories.summary: LA-based apparel company Pistola Denim signed an office lease at ROW DTLA, a 32-acre mixed-use campus with 2 million square feet of space. The denim brand moved its creative team from distribution/warehouse space in Vernon to nearly 18,000 square feet at the property, joining a cluster of fashion, sportswear, and lifestyle brands. ROW DTLA's proximity to LA's Fashion District and Arts District enables this consolidation of creative and retail talent.
stories.impact: Signals creative/fashion companies are trading dispersed warehouse space for branded, collaborative office in mixed-use hubs; downtown LA reurbanization and Arts District gentrification continue to drive demand for boutique office. For multifamily: indicates sustained metro population draw and creative-class migration into DTLA core; supports apartment demand in walkable Arts District and Downtown submarkets. Consider multifamily product near ROW DTLA and along spring Street corridor.

stories.title: New-Construction Vista Strip Center Goes to Institutional Buyer
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets completed the sale of Sunroad Plaza, a 23,540-square-foot retail center at 485 Hacienda Dr. in Vista. The price was not disclosed. Managing directors Daniel Tyner and Jeff Cicurel, alongside senior managing directors Gleb Lvovich and Geoff Tranchina, represented the seller, Sunroad Enterprises. An all-cash institutional investor acquired the asset. Built between 2022 and 2025, Sunroad Plaza is a new construction, 100% occupied strip center leased to nationally recognized quick-service restaurants and retailers. The property includes four drive-thru buildings leased to Starbucks, Chick-fil-A, Panera Bread, The Habit Burger Grill, Jamba Juice and Little Caesars Pizza, along with North County Animal Hospital and BodyBar Pilates. “We continue to experience strong demand for unanchored strip retail due to strong fundamentals, national tenancy and performance,” said Tyner. “Assets like Sunroad Plaza remain highly sought after because they deliver both income stability and future growth potential.” The post New-Construction Vista Strip Center Goes to Institutional Buyer appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sunroad Plaza, 23,540 SF new-construction strip retail in Vista, CA, sold to all-cash institutional buyer.
Built 2022–2025, 100% occupied; QSR anchors (Starbucks, Chick-fil-A, Panera, Habit Burger) plus service tenants.
Strong institutional demand for new-construction, fully-leased retail with national tenancy and drive-thru format.
stories.summary: JLL Capital Markets closed the sale of Sunroad Plaza, a brand-new 23,540-square-foot strip center in Vista, California, to an all-cash institutional investor. The property, completed between 2022 and 2025, is 100% occupied by national QSR brands, including Starbucks, Chick-fil-A, Panera, and The Habit, plus medical and wellness tenants. The deal underscores strong institutional appetite for stabilized new-construction retail with proven national operators.
stories.impact: Reflects institutional capital migrating to unanchored, fully-leased retail with QSR fundamentals and recurring revenue. Limited direct multifamily impact, but signals strong San Diego County North County (Vista) economic confidence and retail spending power; supports nearby multifamily development in growth corridors. Indicates builder confidence in Vista as a delivery market; multifamily feasibility in Vista and Carlsbad submarkets remains viable.

stories.title: A Resilient New York City Wins Big at Commercial Observer’s Power Gala
stories.excerpt: The collective might of New York City real estate was on display Tuesday night, when titans of the industry gathered at 7 World Trade Center to celebrate Commercial Observer’s 19th annual Power Gala. The city’s top developers, brokers and investors enjoyed champagne and petite filet mignon canapés against the backdrop of a 40th-floor skyline view — a landscape many of them had a hand in shaping. Attendees take in the view at the Commercial Observer Power Gala at 7 World Trade Center. PHOTO: Greg Morris/for Commercial Observer While power defines the annual soiree, honorees’ tenacity earned this year’s highest praise. Over the past 12 months, New York City’s commercial real estate sector has made significant strides toward recovering its pre-pandemic vigor, including setting new records for office rents and leasing demand despite interest rate hikes and credit concerns. The 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks also loomed large over the event. The significance of the night’s setting and its host, Silverstein Properties, was not lost on anyone. Joseph Meyer, chairman of Observer Media, remembered witnessing the tragic day’s events as a newly hired analyst at Lehman Brothers, and watching the rebirth of Manhattan in its wake. “This market is defined by rapid evolution,” Meyer said. “And it’s really a privilege to stand in front of you, the executives who have done some of the most transformational transactions in the industry.” CO Editor-in-Chief Max Gross noted that one of Commercial Observer’s first galas following the pandemic was held at 7 World Trade Center. “I think most of the people here tonight understand that whatever bad things come our way — and many have, and there will be other bad things in the future — the answer is to roll up our sleeves and get to work,” Gross said. His words kicked off the night’s awards ceremony, which began with Investment Deal of the Year. Mark Mindick, partner and real estate practice leader at Citrin Coope
bullets: NYC commercial real estate gathered at Commercial Observer Power Gala; Silverstein Properties honored.
NYC office market set new rent records and strong leasing demand despite rate hikes and credit concerns.
Post-pandemic recovery in Manhattan CRE reflects resilience and investor/developer confidence.
stories.summary: New York City's commercial real estate sector was celebrated at Commercial Observer's 19th annual Power Gala at 7 World Trade Center. Over the past 12 months, the sector has recovered significantly pre-pandemic vigor, setting new office rent records and logging strong leasing demand despite higher interest rates and credit market uncertainties. The event underscored industry tenacity and the symbolic importance of downtown Manhattan rebuilding.
stories.impact: Strong office leasing velocity and rent growth in Manhattan signal robust white-collar employment and corporate stability in NYC; supports sustained multifamily demand from young professionals and corporate transfers. However, office strength may channel capital toward office development/conversion, competing with multifamily for scarce development sites and financing in tight Manhattan submarkets. Multifamily developers should prioritize outer-borough and secondary markets (Queens, Brooklyn) where office weakness and demographic demand favor residential.

stories.title: South Florida Starchitect Kobi Karp: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Kobi Karp, founder of Kobi Karp Architecture and Interior Design, has been designing buildings in South Florida for more than three decades. His portfolio includes projects such as Four Seasons at the Surf Club in Surfside, 1 Hotel South Beach, Four Seasons Fort Lauderdale, Wynwood 25 and Moxy Wynwood, and he has worked with many of the region’s most prominent developers over the course of his career. Commercial Observer recently caught up with the star architect to discuss his next big projects, the Live Local Act, and how development in South Florida has changed over the decades. The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What are the big projects on the horizon for your firm? It’s interesting because it’s about 635 units. They leased out 80 percent of the apartments in approximately 80 days. And that is pretty phenomenal, because also the rents are traveling between $5 to $6 a foot. And the demand is substantial, and also what people are seeking in those buildings are amenities and functions that create a lifestyle. The people who rent there are in their early 20s to late 30s. A substantial amount are folks who have jobs in Downtown Miami and are looking to stay there for an extended period of time. So that’s a very interesting sort of scenario. The residents get up in the morning and they go to their offices and then come back in the afternoon. There are activities there for the people who live there, and they also bring their friends over. bullets: Kobi Karp, South Florida starchitect, reports financed multifamily projects leading development pipeline.
Recent Miami River project (Flow operator, 635 units) leased 80% in ~80 days; rents outperforming.
Live Local Act and multifamily financing availability driving South Florida residential development over office/hotel.
stories.summary: Kobi Karp, renowned South Florida architect with 30+ years in the region, reports that financed multifamily apartments dominate his current pipeline ahead of office and hospitality. A recent 635-unit Miami River residential project (Flow-operated) leased 80 percent of units in approximately 80 days at strong rents. Karp attributes the multifamily momentum to favorable financing conditions and the state's Live Local Act incentives.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily market is exceptionally hot; rapid absorption (80% in 80 days) and strong rent trajectory indicate constrained supply and sustained demand inflow (migration, remote workers, corporate relocation). Live Local Act tax incentives are accelerating development velocity. For Trammell Crow: Miami River submarket and Miami-Dade multifamily pipeline offer strong value-add and development opportunity. Competition for land and financing will intensify; prioritize land control in emerging infill submarkets (Wynwood, Allapattah, Little Haiti) before rents and land costs escalate further.

stories.title: BHI Lends $72M on New Jersey Apartments Build
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Prestige Development and Anak Development has landed $71.5 million of construction financing to build a multifamily project in northern New Jersey, Commercial Observer has learned. BHI, the U.S Branch of Bank Hapoalim, provided the loan for the sponsorship’s 250-unit The Standard apartment community in Bayonne, N.J. Maven Capital’s Sean Shahkohi negotiated the financing. David Kesselman, vice president of commercial real estate at BHI, said in a statement that the Bayonne project will “expand the local housing supply and meet growing demand.” Located at 197 Avenue East steps from 22nd Street Station on the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail line, the apartment property will feature a mix of studio to two-bedroom units, a 227-space parking garage and roughly 1,950 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Community amenities will include a swimming pool, sundeck, fitness center, yoga room, sauna, coworking areas, golf simulator and dog walk. Michael Shahkohi, principal of Prestige Development, said in a statement that BHI understood when executing the loan “both the complexity of construction execution and the long-term vision” of the project. The Standard project was designed by MHS Architecture and is situated at the former site of the Villanova Catering Hall. It is slated for completion in summer 2027. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: BHI (Bank Hapoalim US) closes $71.5M construction loan on 250-unit The Standard, Bayonne, NJ.
Prestige Development and Anak Development JV; project at 197 Avenue E near Hudson-Bergen Light Rail 22nd St. Station.
Mixed studio to 2BR, 227-space parking garage, 1,950 SF retail, full amenity package.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Prestige Development and Anak Development secured $71.5 million of construction financing from BHI (Bank Hapoalim US) for The Standard, a 250-unit multifamily project in Bayonne, New Jersey. Located at 197 Avenue East steps from the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail 22nd Street Station, the property will feature studio to 2-bedroom units, a 227-space parking garage, ground-floor retail, and amenities including a pool, fitness center, coworking, and dog walk.
stories.impact: Transit-oriented multifamily financing in Hudson County remains strong; BHI's willingness to deploy $71.5M construction capital for a 250-unit TOD in Bayonne signals healthy NJ multifamily fundamentals and lender confidence in transit-proximate assets. Bayonne waterfront and Light Rail proximity support population growth and young-professional inflow from Manhattan. For Trammell Crow: Hudson County (Bayonne, Jersey City waterfront) remains an undervalued gateway market with strong transit, lower land costs vs. Manhattan, and pent-up housing demand. Consider pre-development in adjacent Jersey City submarkets before capital and land costs escalate.

stories.title: Coworking Firm Industrious to Provide Hologram-Like Google Beam Meetings
stories.excerpt: Industrious, a major flexible workplace company, announced Thursday that it has partnered with Google to launch a network of Google Beam meeting rooms exclusively for its members and guests. Google’s HP Dimension with Google Beam bills itself as an artificial intelligence-first video communication platform that renders meeting participants in their true size, positioned as if they were sitting around the same table. Spatial audio anchors each voice directly to the speaker, so people look, sound and feel more like they’re in the same room without headsets or complex setup, according to the announcement. The rooms will be available in New York City, Chicago, Atlanta and Palo Alto, Calif., starting in October. Industrious locations with Google Beam will include those at Tower 49 in New York City, Ponce City Market in Atlanta, the Ogilvie Transportation Center in Chicago and East Palo Alto. “What makes Beam special is how natural the conversation feels,” Carlos Becil, chief product officer at Industrious, said in an email to Commercial Observer. “The person across from you appears at their true size, their voice comes from where they’re sitting, and you can read the facial expressions and subtle cues that help people connect naturally. “We’re excited about this partnership because it means we can offer our members a face-to-face experience across cities thousands of miles apart,” Becil added. “That is something quite new, and we’re excited to see how our members use it. The rooms with Google Beam are complimentary for Industrious members and bookable for nonmembers. The pricing will be similar to our other bookable conferencing-enabled spaces.” Any Industrious guest can book an HP Dimension with Google Beam session on demand, while Industrious members receive priority scheduling alongside their everyday workspaces and collaboration tools. bullets: Industrious launches Google Beam hologram-like meeting rooms in coworking locations.
Rollout starts October in NYC (Tower 49), Chicago (Ogilvie), Atlanta (Ponce City), Palo Alto (East Palo Alto).
AI-powered spatial video collaboration technology integrated into flexible workplace model.
stories.summary: Industrious, a major coworking operator, announced a partnership with Google to deploy Google Beam meeting rooms—AI-powered spatial video communication rendering participants at true size—across its network starting October. Locations include Tower 49 in New York City, Ponce City Market in Atlanta, the Ogilvie Transportation Center in Chicago, and East Palo Alto, California. The technology aims to replicate in-person meeting dynamics without headsets or complex setup.
stories.impact: Minor relevance to multifamily development. Signals coworking/flexible workspace operators are investing in immersive, on-site collaboration technology to compete with remote work and differentiate product. This may slow tenant migration from flex workspace into traditional office, slightly dampening office-to-residential conversion demand in core urban markets. However, coworking presence in multifamily-dense urban corridors (Tower 49 NYC, Ponce City Atlanta, Ogilvie Chicago) reinforces walkable, mixed-use amenity clusters and supports young-professional renter migration into these submarkets. Neutral-to-slightly-positive signal for multifamily in coworking-anchored neighborhoods.
